output.title: 2026 Global M&A Outlook
output.summary: The report reviews the recovery and changing character of global M&A, using survey findings to frame the 2026 outlook. It examines buyer differences and the effects of market fragmentation, portfolio simplification, AI-enabled deal execution, and execution discipline, followed by industry-specific perspectives and implications for dealmakers.

sections.title: Foreword
sections.summary: Opening remarks introduce the report’s outlook on global M&A.

sections.title: About the research
sections.summary: Describes the survey basis for the report and the composition of its respondents.
key_points: The findings are based on a global survey of corporate respondents.
The report presents respondent composition by geography and corporate industry.

sections.title: Executive summary
sections.summary: Summarizes a recovering M&A market whose foundations have shifted, with consequences for deal execution and value creation.
key_points: Global M&A momentum is rebuilding, but the market’s foundations have changed.
Deal activity regained momentum through 2025.
The report characterizes the global market as multi-speed.

sections.title: 2025 retrospective and 2026 outlook
sections.summary: Reviews the return of M&A momentum and the varying conditions facing dealmakers in the United States and elsewhere.
key_points: Momentum has returned with greater selectivity.
US dealmakers are described as setting the pace in a multi-speed market.
Dealmakers outside the US face a more complex mix of conditions.

sections.title: 5 drivers shaping the 2026 M&A environment
sections.summary: Introduces the report’s five-driver framework for the 2026 M&A environment and leads into the following thematic sections.
key_points: The framework includes strategic focus in a fragmented world.
The following themes address buyer risk appetites, portfolio simplification, AI-driven deal execution, and execution discipline.

sections.title: Strategic focus in a fragmented world
sections.summary: Explores strategic focus amid fragmentation and presents regional differences in M&A outlook.
key_points: The section presents outlook categories ranging from much higher to slightly or much lower.
It compares regional views for APAC, EMEA, and the Americas.

sections.title: Diverging risk appetites between buyers
sections.summary: Examines differences in risk appetite across buyer groups, including corporate and private equity respondents.
key_points: Buyer risk appetite is treated as a source of divergence in the M&A environment.
The section includes comparisons between corporate and private equity respondents.

sections.title: Portfolio simplification as a value creation strategy
sections.summary: Considers portfolio simplification as a route to value creation through changes to the composition of businesses and assets.
key_points: Portfolio simplification is framed as a value creation strategy.

sections.title: AI-driven transformation of deal execution
sections.summary: Discusses how AI is changing deal execution and analytical capacity while emphasizing that execution risks remain.
key_points: AI expands analytical capacity and reshapes asset attractiveness.
AI does not eliminate execution risk.
The report says AI raises the bar for governance, integration readiness, and institutional discipline.

sections.title: Execution discipline as a decisive source of advantage
sections.summary: Frames disciplined execution as a source of advantage in M&A.
key_points: Execution discipline is presented as a decisive source of advantage.

sections.title: Industry-specific dynamics
sections.summary: Compares portfolio and execution considerations across industries, including consumer and retail, banking and insurance, and natural resources, energy, and chemicals.
key_points: Consumer and retail portfolio reshaping responds to margin pressure, changing demand, and the need for greater operational focus; execution risks include customer experience and frontline talent.
Banking and insurance activity emphasizes selective divestments and capability-driven acquisitions, with execution risks around regulatory approvals, data migration, and platform integration.
In natural resources, energy, and chemicals, carve-outs can manage exposure and release capital; asset specificity, regulatory continuity, and longer timelines amplify execution risk.

sections.title: Implications for dealmakers
sections.summary: The closing section addresses what the report’s outlook and themes mean for dealmakers.
